sentences.text: The primary fossil evidence for Hesperonychus is a partial pelvic girdle known as the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — UALVP 48778.
A series of very small toe bones, including sickle claws, in the Royal Tyrrell Museum collection may also belong to this animal.
Despite its small size, the fused pubic bones indicate the specimen is an adult and not a juvenile of a known species.
Hesperonychus is the smallest known non-avian carnivorous dinosaur from North America and the first microraptor described in that region.
It was the first small carnivorous theropod found at the site, weighing less than 10 kg.
The animal appears to have been a common feature of the Dinosaur Park Formation environment, with at least ten distinct specimens found compared to fewer remains of other small carnivores.
The species Hesperonychus elizabethae was named in honor of Dr. Elizabeth Nicholls, who collected the fossils as a student in 1982.
The species was described by Nicholas R. Longrich and Philip J. Currie in 2009 and is the only species in the genus.
Hesperonychus was assigned to Microraptoria based on features including a spatulate pubic symphysis, a curved pubic shaft, and lateral tubercules expanded into wing-like structures.
Longrich and Currie concluded Hesperonychus likely did not have four wings or glide like Microraptor, but was more similar in behavior to Sinornithosaurus.
Hesperonychus belongs to the family Dromaeosauridae and is classified in the class Reptilia.

Longrich and Currie classified Hesperonychus as a member of the Microraptorinae, a group previously thought to be restricted to the Early Cretaceous of Asia, and the parent group of Hesperonychus is Microraptorinae.
In 2012, Martyniuk classified Hesperonychus as a eudromaeosaurian.
In 2019, Hartman and colleagues suggested Hesperonychus was an avialan close to modern birds, though they disagreed with the classification of microraptorines as avialans.
In 2020, Hesperonychus was recovered as a dromaeosaurid that was a sister taxon to, but not a member of, the microraptorines.
In 2014, Brusatte and colleagues excluded Hesperonychus from phylogenetic analyses due to a lack of data, indicating its classification remains uncertain.
The gracile appearance of associated toe bones suggests Hesperonychus likely did not belong to the Eudromaeosauria.
Hesperonychus lived around 75 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in Alberta, Canada, where fossils were found in the Dinosaur Park Formation.
Hesperonychus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
The discovery of Hesperonychus in the Late Cretaceous Campanian extends the fossil range of microraptorines by 45 million years compared to the previously known Late Aptian Microraptor.
It is debated whether dinosaur competition prevented mammals from growing larger, if mammal competition allowed dinosaurs to remain tiny, or if both factors were at play.
